suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The public group members route now calls `model.findMembers()`, which asks for only `limit: 50` (the model default), and the public members.hbs template has no paging controls. WHY: Non-automatic groups used to return all members. Now any group with more than 50 members shows only the first 50 on the public page, and users cannot see the rest. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `limit` and `offset` come from user params and are passed to SQL without bounds or sign checks. This public endpoint now applies them to every group, not only automatic groups. WHY: A negative value (e.g. `limit=-1`) makes PostgreSQL raise 'LIMIT must not be negative', which returns a 500, and a very large limit loads every member. suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: totalPages uses floor(count/limit)+1, so it reports one page too many when user_count is an exact multiple of limit.

suggestions.label: bug

suggestions.label: bug

Very large limits are also accepted. Clamp the values, for example `limit = [[params[:limit].to_i, 1].max, 200].min` and `offset = [params[:offset].to_i, 0].max`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Fallback locales are only loaded through FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!, and the only caller is ApplicationController#set_locale. The patched I18n.translate (translate_accelerator.rb:68) lazily loads only config.locale. In code paths that don't go through a controller (Sidekiq jobs, mailers using I18n.with_locale, rake tasks, console), the :en and site-default translations are never loaded, so I18n::Backend::Fallbacks finds nothing and returns 'translation missing' instead of falling back. Fix: call the fallback loading in the patched translate, e.g. `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].each { |l| ensure_loaded!(l) }` (or on locale change), not only in the controller.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The fallback chain now depends on SiteSetting.default_locale, which can change at runtime. But the translation LRU cache in translate_accelerator.rb:72 is keyed only by key+config.locale+backend.object_id. After an admin changes default_locale, strings already cached through the old site-locale fallback keep being served (stale/wrong-language text) until the process restarts or reload! runs. Fix: include the fallback chain or SiteSetting.default_locale in the cache key, or clear @cache when default_locale changes.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Fallback locales load only in ApplicationController, so on other paths a 'translation missing' fallback result gets cached under the real key.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
With Fallbacks enabled, a key missing from the user's locale is resolved from SiteSetting.default_locale or :en. But `I18n.translate` (translate_accelerator.rb:68) only lazy-loads `config.locale`, and the fallback locales are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in ApplicationController.

In jobs, mailers, rake tasks, or anywhere else that sets I18n.locale, the fallback locale may not be loaded yet. The lookup then returns a 'translation missing' string. That string is frozen and stored in the LRU cache under the same key a correct lookup would use (translate_accelerator.rb:72-76), so every later caller gets the failure, even after the fallback locale is loaded.

The cache key also doesn't include the site default locale. After the default locale changes, the cache keeps returning stale fallback text.

Fix: inside `translate`, load every locale in `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]`, for example by calling `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in place of the single `load_locale` call. Also include the fallback chain (or at least SiteSetting.default_locale) in the cache key.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Fallbacks need the whole locale chain loaded, but the lazy `translate` still loads only `config.locale`. Outside controllers, fallback lookups miss and the miss gets cached.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
Fallbacks now expect the site-default and :en translations to be loaded. The lazy-loading `translate` was not updated for this: it still loads only `config.locale`. The fallback chain gets loaded only in `ApplicationController#set_locale` (`I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`).

Any `I18n.t` call outside a controller request runs without the fallback locales loaded. That includes Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks and the console. So a key missing in the user's locale returns "translation missing" instead of falling back.

That result is then frozen into the LRU cache under `key+locale+backend_id`. It stays wrong even after the fallback locales load later.

Suggested fix: load the full chain inside `translate`, e.g. `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].each { |l| ensure_loaded!(l) }`, in place of `load_locale(config.locale)`. The controller then won't need to call it separately.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Fallbacks only work where the controller preloads them; `translate` loads only the current locale, so fallback lookups elsewhere miss and the miss gets cached.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
config/initializers/i18n.rb turns on `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` with the chain `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en]`, which assumes all of those locales are loaded. This lazy loader only loads `config.locale` in `translate`. Fallback locales are only loaded through `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`, and only `ApplicationController#set_locale` calls that.

In background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, or any other code that sets `I18n.locale` and calls `I18n.t`, a key missing from the user's locale falls back to `:en` or the site locale. That locale was never loaded, so the result is "translation missing", and `translate` caches that result in the LRU cache.

Fix: load the whole fallback chain inside `translate`, so callers don't have to remember to do it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Fallback locales are only loaded in the controller hook, so outside a request (jobs, mailers, rake) fallbacks look in locales that were never loaded and return missing-translation text.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Fallbacks only work when the fallback locales have been loaded, and today only the controller hook loads them. When a background job, mailer or rake task translates a key that is missing from the current locale, the fallback lookup reaches a site-default or :en locale that was never loaded. It returns 'translation missing' instead of the fallback text, and that result is then cached. Move the loading into `translate` so it always happens, e.g. `I18n.fallbacks[config.locale].each { |l| ensure_loaded!(l) }` instead of loading only `config.locale`. Then the controller-specific call isn't needed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: ProvideAnonDBStore now needs an extra `deviceLimit int64` argument, but pkg/server/wire.go:374-375 still registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), new(*anonstore.AnonDBStore))`. WHY: Wire has no int64 provider, so dependency-injection codegen fails. Even if it could resolve one, ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now builds the store itself (impl.go:43), which leaves the provider unused, and wire rejects that too. The server stops building. HOW: Remove ProvideAnonDBStore and the AnonStore bind from wire.go. Alternatively, make the provider take *setting.Cfg and keep injecting AnonStore into ProvideAnonymousDeviceService.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: TagDevice now returns the tagDeviceUI error, but tagDeviceUI writes the localCache key (impl.go:87) before CreateOrUpdateDevice runs and never removes it when the write fails. WHY: When the device limit is reached, the first request fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached (client.go:45-46). Every later request from the same device ID in the next 29 minutes hits the cache, gets nil back and authenticates, so the limit only blocks one request per cache window. HOW: Write the cache entry only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or call `a.localCache.Delete(key)` when it returns an error.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The device limit is enforced as a check-then-act: CountDevices, then a separate INSERT/upsert, with no transaction, lock or DB constraint. WHY: Now that TagDevice runs synchronously per request, concurrent requests from new devices (or several Grafana instances) can all read `count < deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the configured limit is exceeded. HOW: Run the count and insert in one transaction with appropriate locking. Alternatively, make the insert conditional in SQL (e.g. INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?) and check rows affected.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Anonymous auth is now refused only when the client-supplied X-Grafana-Device-Id header maps to an over-limit device. TagDevice returns nil when the header is missing (impl.go:120-121), and any new random value counts toward the shared limit. WHY: An anonymous client can skip the limit by leaving the header out. An unauthenticated attacker can also send many random device IDs to fill `device_limit`. After that, every legitimate new anonymous viewer gets an auth error until the fake devices age out after 30 days. That is a cheap denial of service against anonymous access. HOW: Don't key enforcement only on an untrusted header: reject requests that omit it when a limit is set, and consider rate-limiting new device registrations per client IP.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: TagDevice used to run in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. It now runs synchronously inside Authenticate. With a limit set, each local-cache miss runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ...` over a 30-day window plus an upsert or update. WHY: Every anonymous request from a new device ID now pays at least two DB round trips during authentication, and the COUNT grows with the number of devices. Floods of unique device IDs turn into one full-range COUNT per request on the auth hot path, with no timeout. HOW: Keep the count check but cache the device count briefly (or keep it in memory and refresh it periodically) instead of querying on every new-device request. Restore a bounded context for the DB work.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: ProvideAnonDBStore now needs an int64, but pkg/server/wire.go still lists it as a wire provider, so wire can't build the dependency graph.
suggestions.suggestionContent: ProvideAnonDBStore now takes a deviceLimit int64, and ProvideAnonymousDeviceService builds the store itself. But pkg/server/wire.go:374-375 still registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), new(*anonstore.AnonDBStore))`. Wire has no provider for the int64 parameter, so wire generation and the server build fail. Remove both entries from wire.go (and from any other wire sets like wireexts), or keep a wire-compatible constructor that reads the limit from *setting.Cfg.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: ProvideAnonDBStore now needs an int64 device limit, but wire.go still registers it as a provider, and wire cannot supply a bare int64.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The PR changes `ProvideAnonDBStore` to `(db.DB, int64)` and makes `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` build the store directly. The wire set in `pkg/server/wire.go` (lines 374-375) still registers `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` and binds `AnonStore` to it. Nothing provides an `int64`, so wire generation fails with an unsatisfied dependency, and the server can't be built. Remove the `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` provider and the `AnonStore` bind from `wire.go`, since the service now creates the store with `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`. Alternatively, keep a wire-compatible constructor that takes `*setting.Cfg` and reads `AnonymousDeviceLimit` from it.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The device limit check counts first and inserts later with nothing tying the two together, so concurrent new devices can push the count past the limit.
suggestions.suggestionContent: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices and then, in a separate statement, the upsert. There is no transaction, lock or DB constraint around the two steps. Anonymous Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously on each request (client.go:44). N concurrent requests from different new devices can therefore all read count < deviceLimit and all insert, leaving more than device_limit devices registered. To enforce the limit, do the check and the insert atomically: for example, use a conditional INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?, or run both inside a serialized transaction or under a lock.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: updateDevice changes `args` inside a callback that WithDbSession may run again, so a retry calls Exec with the query string in the arguments twice.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` reassigns the captured `args` variable inside the WithDbSession callback. When SQLite reports the database is locked, WithDbSession re-runs the callback (sqlstore/session.go:83 retryOnLocks). On that retry the query is prepended again, so Exec receives [query, query, ip, ua, ...]. The extra argument shifts every bind value, and the statement errors instead of updating the device. Build the argument slice in a new local variable inside the callback, e.g. `execArgs := append([]interface{}{query}, args...)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The device limit only blocks a new device's first request, because the local cache key is written before the store call and kept when it fails.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The device limit is only enforced on a new device's first request. tagDeviceUI caches the device key before it calls CreateOrUpdateDevice and keeps the key when the call fails. After the first ErrDeviceLimitReached, every request from that device in the next ~29 minutes hits the cache, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate lets the device in. Fix: set the cache key only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or delete it when the call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The `updateDevice` doc comment refers to "the given times", but the function takes none and also hides that a miss returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says the update applies to devices 'updated between the given times', but `updateDevice` accepts no time arguments. It derives a fixed window from `device.UpdatedAt` (`anonymousDeviceExpiration` before it to one minute after it). The comment also leaves out that if no matching row exists, the function returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. A caller reading the comment would expect to pass a time range and would not expect a limit error. Suggested rewording: "updateDevice updates an existing device seen within anonymousDeviceExpiration of device.UpdatedAt; returns ErrDeviceLimitReached if no such device exists."

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: rowsAffected==0 is used to mean 'device not found', but on MySQL a matched row with unchanged values also returns 0, so an existing device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached.
suggestions.suggestionContent: updateDevice reads a 0 from RowsAffected as 'this device is not registered' and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected counts only rows that actually changed, not rows that matched. That case happens when the limit is already reached and a known device sends two requests in the same second (updated_at has second precision) with the same client_ip and user_agent. The UPDATE matches the row but changes nothing, so it returns 0. The legitimate device then gets ErrDeviceLimitReached, and client.go now turns that into an authentication failure. Fix: when the UPDATE affects 0 rows, check whether the row exists, e.g. `SELECT 1 FROM anon_device WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?`. Return ErrDeviceLimitReached only if that query finds nothing.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: On MySQL, a device that already exists can get ErrDeviceLimitReached when its update changes no values.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `rowsAffected == 0` is used to mean "device not found", but on MySQL it can also mean "found, but no values changed". That happens when a device repeats a request in the same second with the same IP and user agent. A device that is already registered would then be rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached. Fix: check whether the device exists with a separate query, or don't rely on rows-affected semantics for this decision.

suggestions.label: testing
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Add a test that an existing device can still be updated after the device limit is reached.
suggestions.suggestionContent: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit sets limit=1, inserts one device, then sends a different device ID. It confirms that a new device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached, so it does catch removal of the limit check. It does not check that an already-known device can still be updated once the limit is reached. Add a case that re-sends the original device ID after the limit is hit and asserts that the update succeeds. This is a coverage gap, not a test that claims something it doesn't verify.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: After taking the write lock (line 48), the code does not check entryPointAssetsCache again. When several requests miss the cache at the same time, each one queues on Lock() and then re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json in turn, even after the first one has filled the cache. WHY: GetWebAssets runs on every index page load (pkg/api/index.go:82) and frontend-settings request (pkg/api/frontendsettings.go:62). At startup, or whenever the manifest fails to load (line 69 then stores nil, so every call misses again), all those requests run one at a time behind a global exclusive lock doing file I/O and JSON decoding. In Dev mode every call takes the exclusive lock. HOW: Re-check the cache right after Lock(): `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Also consider not overwriting a good cached value with nil when loading fails.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: There is no second cache check after taking the write lock, so concurrent misses each rebuild and overwrite the cache.
suggestions.suggestionContent: There is a gap between RUnlock (line 43) and Lock (line 48). Every goroutine that finds the cache empty will wait for the write lock and then rebuild the assets. Each one re-reads and re-parses the manifest and replaces the cached pointer, even though an earlier goroutine already filled it. To fix this, check the cache again once the write lock is held.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: instrumentContext is the first production caller of log.WithContextualAttributes. That function does `append(ctx.Value(logParamsContextKey{}).([]any), logParams...)` on the slice stored in the parent context, and the slice built here with `append` can have spare capacity (e.g. len 8/10, cap 12). WHY: when a plugin request is made with a ctx that already went through this middleware (nested plugin calls, or several goroutines fanning out from one instrumented ctx), the append writes into the shared backing array. Concurrent calls race and can overwrite each other's endpoint/pluginId/dsUID/uname attributes, and nested calls also log duplicate endpoint/pluginId keys. HOW: store a copy with exact capacity, e.g. `p = slices.Clip(p)` before calling WithContextualAttributes, or (preferably) change WithContextualAttributes to build a new slice (`append(append(make([]any,0,len(old)+len(new)), old...), new...)`).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver. WHY: LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs only through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a TestLogger to assert on 'Plugin Request Completed' will see zero InfoLogs calls. Logging assertions become impossible and a regression in the logger middleware would go undetected. HOW: return the receiver (`return f`) so calls are recorded on the logger the test holds.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The test function still uses the old InstrumentationMiddleware name, but it tests the renamed MetricsMiddleware.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Rename `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` to `TestMetricsMiddleware` so it matches the middleware it tests. With the old name, someone searching for MetricsMiddleware tests won't find it, and the name refers to a type that no longer exists.

suggestions.label: testing
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Add a negative assertion that request size is not recorded for CheckHealth and CollectMetrics.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The test never asserts that the request-size metric is absent for the CheckHealth and CollectMetrics endpoints. The implementation is correct, so this is only a missing negative check, not an incorrect assertion. Adding it would catch a regression that starts recording request size for these endpoints.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The async legacy writes in Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) get their timeout context from the request ctx, which the apiserver cancels as soon as the handler returns. WHY: Usually the legacy write is cancelled right after the response is sent, so the legacy store silently stops getting creates, updates and deletes and falls out of sync, which defeats the 'safe measure' purpose of mode 3. Legacy errors are also never logged, only counted in metrics. HOW: Use `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), 10*time.Second, ...)` so values such as the identity are kept but the request's cancellation is not, and call `log.Error` when the legacy call fails.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Legacy Update now gets the caller's original objInfo instead of the earlier updateWrapper that carried the object Unified Storage produced. WHY: Legacy recomputes the update (patch, preconditions, resourceVersion) against its own old copy, so the update can fail on a resourceVersion or precondition mismatch, or produce a different object from Unified Storage. The stores then diverge with no log. HOW: Wrap the result as before: `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Metrics are recorded with the wrong helper or the wrong label. Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) report a Unified Storage failure through recordLegacyDuration. Delete success (line 106) passes `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label. The DeleteCollection goroutine (line 166) records the legacy call with recordStorageDuration. Delete (line 97) also puts d.Log into the ctx instead of the enriched `log`. WHY: Storage errors show up as legacy errors, legacy delete-collection latency is counted as storage, and putting object names in a label creates unbounded label cardinality. Together these make the dual-writer dashboards misleading. HOW: Use recordStorageDuration at lines 45 and 129, options.Kind at line 106, recordLegacyDuration at line 166, and `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` at line 97.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: The goroutine passes the same `obj` pointer to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has already used it. Storage.Create may have mutated it (UID, resourceVersion), and it may be the same object that the handler is serializing concurrently. WHY: Legacy can receive Unified Storage metadata, and concurrent access to the object can cause a data race. HOW: Pass `obj.DeepCopyObject()` into the goroutine.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Legacy writes now run in unordered goroutines, so writes to the same object can reach legacy storage in a different order than the client sent them.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Mode 3 now starts each legacy write (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) in its own goroutine and returns at once. Nothing keeps those writes in the order the client sent them. Example: a client creates X and gets a response, then deletes X. If the legacy Delete goroutine runs before the legacy Create goroutine, the delete fails with NotFound, the create then succeeds, and X stays in legacy storage even though it was deleted. Two updates in a row can likewise leave legacy with an older version. Either keep the legacy write synchronous, as before this PR, or send legacy writes through a per-object (or per-resource) queue or lock so they run in the order they were issued.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete passes the resource name instead of the kind as the metric label to recordStorageDuration, causing incorrect labels and high cardinality.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In Delete, the resource `name` is passed as the kind label to `recordStorageDuration`. This puts individual resource names into a Prometheus label, which makes the label incorrect (it should be the kind) and creates a cardinality problem. The reviewer noted it is not a sensitive-data exposure, so it was outside their data-exposure assignment.

suggestions.label: maintainability
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete stores d.Log in the context instead of the enriched logger, so downstream logs lose contextual fields.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Delete puts the base `d.Log` logger into the context instead of the enriched logger. Downstream logging loses the contextual fields such as kind, name, method and mode. It does not expose any sensitive data.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Create failure in unified storage is recorded as legacy duration.
suggestions.suggestionContent: When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) with startStorage. That times the unified-storage call but adds it to the legacy histogram, so storage error metrics undercount and legacy metrics get bogus errors. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Update failure in unified storage is recorded as legacy duration.
suggestions.suggestionContent: When d.Storage.Update fails, the timing is sent to recordLegacyDuration even though the measured operation was the storage update. Use recordStorageDuration. The same mix-up happens in reverse at line 166: the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls recordStorageDuration with startLegacy, but it should call recordLegacyDuration.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete success metric is labeled with the object name instead of the kind.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Every other call passes options.Kind as the metric's name label, but the Delete success path passes `name` (the object name). This puts per-object values into the label, which can blow up label cardinality, and it breaks consistency with the error path at line 103 and the legacy path at line 113.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched `log`.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Delete builds `log` with the name, kind and method values, but then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). Downstream storage code that reads the logger from the context therefore does not get those values. Every other method passes `log`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Mode3 writes to legacy storage in a background goroutine tied to the request context, but the new Mode3 playlist integration tests read the legacy API immediately and expect it to match.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In Mode3, Create, Update (lines 134-141), Delete (108-114) and DeleteCollection (161-167) now write to legacy storage in a goroutine and return without waiting. That goroutine uses a context derived from the request, so the legacy write can be cancelled once the response is sent. The new Mode3 integration tests in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (lines 132-204) run doPlaylistTests. That suite creates and updates through k8s, then immediately reads `/api/playlists` and expects the same result. Because nothing guarantees the legacy write has finished (or succeeded), those tests are racy and legacy data can silently diverge. Fix: run the legacy write on a detached context (e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`). Then either make the tests poll or wait until legacy catches up, or keep the legacy write synchronous until the tests are changed to accept eventual consistency.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The background legacy writes in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection (lines 50-57, 108-114, 134-141, 161-167) build their timeout context from the request `ctx`. The apiserver cancels that context soon after the handler returns. So the 10s timeout gives no protection: the legacy Create/Update/Delete is often cancelled partway through or before it starts. Unified storage has already committed by then, so the legacy store silently diverges from it. Derive the context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), ...)` to keep request values but drop the parent's cancellation.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Update used to wrap objInfo in `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}`, so legacy stored exactly the object that unified storage produced. Mode1 and mode2 still do this. Now the raw objInfo goes to Legacy.Update, which re-applies the patch or transform to legacy's own current object, and does so asynchronously. If an earlier async write hasn't landed yet or legacy has drifted, the two stores end up with different contents. Pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` to Legacy.Update.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: This is a data race. In Create, `obj` (which Storage.Create may have mutated, or which may be the same pointer as `created`) goes to Legacy.Create in a goroutine while the same object is returned to the caller. The legacy store can mutate metadata such as resourceVersion, uid and annotations while the response encoder is serializing `created`. That can corrupt the response or panic on a concurrent map access. Give the goroutine its own copy with obj.DeepCopyObject().

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The 'unified store fails' Create case only sets up the legacy mock, and because the mock is shared, that legacy expectation is what makes the storage call fail.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' only registers a Create expectation in setupLegacyFn and has no setupStorageFn. legacyStoreMock and storageMock wrap the same *mock.Mock `m` (storage_mocks_test.go:14-19, 32, 96), so DualWriterMode3.Create's Storage.Create call (dualwriter_mode3.go:42) is answered by the expectation meant for the legacy store. The test would still pass if mode 3 read from legacy instead of storage. Fix: use separate mocks for each store and put the failing expectation in setupStorageFn.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The mode-3 write tests never check the asynchronous legacy write, so they still pass with the legacy writes removed.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Mode 3 is defined as writing to both stores, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection now do the legacy write in a goroutine (dualwriter_mode3.go:50-57, 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). The tests return right after the storage call. They never call AssertExpectations and never wait for the goroutine. The Delete and DeleteCollection cases don't set up a legacy expectation at all, so the goroutine hits an unexpected mock call that can panic or be lost depending on timing. Removing the legacy writes would leave every test green. Fix: use separate legacy mocks, wait on a condition (for example, assert.Eventually on legacy AssertCalled), and assert that the legacy call happened.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Delete used to tolerate `apierrors.IsNotFound` from Storage.Delete and still delete from legacy (also ignoring NotFound there). Now any storage error, NotFound included, is returned right away and the legacy delete is skipped. In mode 3, an object written before the switch exists only in legacy storage. Deleting it now fails with 404 and the legacy copy stays behind. Bring back the NotFound fallback: on NotFound, still delete from legacy and only return the error if the legacy delete also fails. Mode2 keeps NotFound checks (dualwriter_mode2.go:246/257).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: The old Update passed `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` to Legacy.Update, so legacy got exactly the object that unified storage had stored. The new code passes the raw `objInfo`, so legacy re-runs UpdatedObject against its own copy. That copy can have a different resourceVersion or old state, so legacy can now reject the update (conflict or precondition failure) or store a different object, and the stores drift apart. Mode1 and mode2 still wrap the update (dualwriter_mode2.go:298, dualwriter_mode1.go:250). Wrap `res` from Storage.Update in updateWrapper before calling Legacy.Update.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: Legacy writes used to run synchronously within the request. They now run in a goroutine whose context comes from the request `ctx`. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: Removing the function-wide cacheMu lock and locking only the final `b.cache[key] = idx` lets BuildIndex run at the same time for the same key. getOrCreateIndex (search.go:292-298) checks with GetIndex and then calls build without holding any lock, and it is called from concurrent Search/federated search requests and from handleEvent. WHY: Two callers that miss the cache each run a full ListIterator over the resource and build separate indexes. The last writer wins, and the losing index is never closed, so its handle and memory leak. Writes that went into the losing index are lost. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory, so one fails or they corrupt each other. HOW: Add per-key build deduplication, for example singleflight.Group keyed on NamespacedResource, or re-check the cache under the lock and close the duplicate index if another build already stored one.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: With the global lock removed, the errgroup workers in searchSupport.init (search.go:186-192) now actually run BuildIndex in parallel. They all write the same captured `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed++` with no synchronisation. WHY: This is a data race that the serialising lock used to hide. The `go test -race` detector will flag it, and the span attribute count can be wrong. HOW: Use a goroutine-local variable (`_, _, err := s.build(...)`; `return err`) and an atomic counter for totalBatchesIndexed.

suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new postgres skip makes the storage-server integration test pass even if the server is broken on postgres, in the same PR that makes NewResourceServer run Init eagerly.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This PR makes NewResourceServer call s.Init(ctx) during construction (server.go:258), which runs search index init and the watcher, and at the same time skips this test on postgres. When skipped, the test passes even if InitializeModuleServer or the storage server fails on postgres, so a regression caused by the new eager Init can't be caught. The likely cause of the Drone failure is that the postgres branch hardcodes db_host="localhost" (lines 75-79), while the mysql branch reads the host from the connection string because localhost doesn't work in Drone. Fix the config the same way (take host, name, user and password from cfg's [database] section) and remove the skip, rather than turning the postgres run into a guaranteed pass.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: NewResourceServer now runs Init eagerly and fails if it fails, which changes the constructor contract for existing callers that were not updated.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `NewResourceServer` used to be a cheap constructor, with initialization done lazily or explicitly through `Init` (lifecycle hooks, search index build, watcher). It now calls `s.Init(ctx)` inside the constructor and returns `nil, err` if that fails. The existing callers were not changed: sql/server.go:77, client.go:67, apistore/restoptions.go:52/87 and registry/apis/dashboard/legacy_storage.go:28. Effects on them: (1) a lifecycle or backend init failure, or a search index build failure, now makes construction fail and blocks Grafana startup. Before, the server was returned and `Init` errors surfaced per request. (2) The whole index build now runs synchronously inside every constructor call. (3) `Init` runs with the server's internal 'watcher' admin context, not the caller's context. Because of `sync.Once`, the caller's later `Init(ctx)` is ignored. Either keep `Init` lazy or explicit, or update the callers to expect blocking construction that can fail, and handle the error or degrade gracefully, for example by treating search as optional.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock lets two concurrent builds of the same key both run, and the last one to finish overwrites the cached index.
suggestions.suggestionContent: cacheMu now protects only the final map write. getOrCreateIndex (search.go:287-306) checks the cache and then builds without holding any lock. So two concurrent callers for the same NamespacedResource (for example the watch goroutine in handleEvent and a request path) can both see a miss and both call BuildIndex. Each builds its own index, and the last one to finish overwrites `b.cache[key]`. Any documents written to the overwritten index through handleEvent are silently dropped. For file-based indexes, the second `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory fails. Fix: after acquiring the lock, check whether `b.cache[key]` is already set and return that index instead of overwriting it. Better still, deduplicate builds per key, e.g. with singleflight or a per-key mutex in getOrCreateIndex.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Now that index builds really run in parallel, init's errgroup goroutines race on the shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In searchSupport.init (search.go:186-193), each goroutine runs `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` on variables captured from the enclosing function. While BuildIndex held cacheMu for its whole duration, builds were effectively serialized. With the lock removed, they run in parallel, which creates a real data race on `err` and on the counter. For example, one goroutine's nil can overwrite another goroutine's error before group.Wait. Use a goroutine-local `err` (`_, _, err := s.build(...)`) and an atomic counter.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: isAccessTokenId reads `items[0].substring(3, 5)`, but the encoder puts the grant shortcut at characters 4-6 (sessionType 0-2, tokenType 2-4, grant 4-6). A token with the wrong grant shortcut still passes, and a correct one passes only because the wrong substring never equals the shortcut. So the event assertions in expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken give no regression coverage. suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `getShortcut()` is a new abstract SPI method with no default. Its contract says 'usually like 3-letters', but DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId requires the encoded context to be exactly 6 chars (2+2+2). Nothing validates the shortcut's length or non-null value. WHY: Existing custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations no longer compile, or hit AbstractMethodError at runtime. A custom shortcut that is not 2 chars produces access-token IDs that the decoder rejects with IllegalArgumentException. A null shortcut makes `grantsByShortcuts.put(null, ...)` in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit throw an NPE, because ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys, and server startup fails. HOW: Document and enforce a 2-character, non-null shortcut (validate it in postInit and in getShortcutByGrantType). Consider a default implementation so existing providers still compile.

suggestions.label: bug

For the prefix "onrtac", substring(3,5) gives "ta", which mixes the token-type and grant characters. On top of that, the check returns false when the segment *equals* the expected shortcut. So in practice the matcher accepts any well-formed ID with any grant type, and the new test assertions in expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken and expectAuthReqIdToToken check nothing about the grant. Use substring(4,6) and return false when the segment does *not* equal the expected shortcut.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The isAccessTokenId matcher reads the wrong substring and inverts the comparison, so it never checks the grant shortcut.

It also returns false when the slice *matches* the expected shortcut instead of when it differs. As a result, token IDs with any grant (including "na" when the GRANT_TYPE attribute is never set) pass `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, the device-code check and the CIBA check. Fix: check `items[0].length() == 6` and `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.

suggestions.label: bug

After `deletedAll.set(true)`, the assertion on `caughtExceptions` runs straight away, while the reader may still be partway through `groups(...)`. suggestions.suggestionContent: getClientsWithPermission searches with findByType(server, "Clients"), but per-client resources are created by AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource without a type (resourceStore.create(server, name, owner)). Its caller, AvailableRoleMappingResource.getRoleIdsWithPermissions, runs realm.getClientById(cid).getRolesStream() on each id, so it throws a NullPointerException for "Clients". suggestions.suggestionContent: When a client has no resource of its own, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(..., CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) without a null check. suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent:
**What:** PasswordForm.authenticate now calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm whenever context.getUser() has a passkey. In a UsernameForm -> PasswordForm flow, that user was identified only by a username typed into the form. fillContextForm puts ALLOWED_AUTHENTICATORS (the user's WebAuthn credential IDs) and IS_USER_IDENTIFIED=true on the form, and the new passkeys.ftl block writes every credential ID into hidden `authn_use_chk` inputs.

**Why it matters:** an unauthenticated visitor can type any username and learn whether that account has passkeys, plus its stable WebAuthn credential IDs. Those IDs can be used to track users or to target phishing at a specific authenticator. Before this change, the password step in this flow showed no passkey data; the old tests asserted the webauthn form was absent.

**Fix:** only fill identified-user WebAuthn data during real re-authentication, i.e. when the user was set by an earlier authenticated session, as with USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH. Otherwise, render conditional UI without allowCredentials (as when user == null) so credential IDs are not exposed.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Password page now shows any typed username's passkey credential IDs, and whether the account has a passkey, to an unauthenticated visitor.
suggestions.suggestionContent:
In the username-form → password-form flow, the user is identified only by the username that was typed; they haven't authenticated yet. With this change, `PasswordForm.authenticate` (and `UsernamePasswordForm`) calls `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` for that user. The new `passkeys.ftl` block then writes all of the user's WebAuthn credential IDs into the HTML as hidden `authn_use_chk` inputs. The `#webauth` form is also rendered only when the user has a passkey.

This lets anyone who types a username:
- learn whether that account has passkeys, and
- read its credential IDs, which are stable per-authenticator identifiers that can be used to track a device across sites.

Previously the password page showed no WebAuthn data. The fix is needed for re-authentication, where the user is already authenticated (USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH). Consider one of these:
- Populate the per-user authenticators list only in that re-authentication case.
- In the normal flow, keep passkeys discoverable (conditional UI, with no allowCredentials list), so the page looks the same whether or not the user exists or has a passkey.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` compares an org-aware wrapped `original` (from `getById`) with the raw `updated` model. The wrapper's isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled, but the cached login ID lists come from `idpDelegate.getForLogin` and ignore org state. WHY: while an org is disabled, its public IDPs stay in the cached ORG_ONLY/ALL lists. If an admin then updates one of them to hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true or BROKER_PUBLIC=false, both sides fail the predicate and the first early return skips invalidation. After the org is re-enabled, the stale ID passes the bean's isEnabled() re-check and the hidden/private IDP appears on the login page. HOW: evaluate the original with the stored, unwrapped state, e.g. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(idpDelegate.getById(model.getInternalId()), model)`. Alternatively, always invalidate when the original is org-linked.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes nodestore.get_multi returns values in the same order and count as error_ids, but it doesn't. get_multi (nodestore/base.py:184-205) deduplicates ids, builds the result from uncached ids first, then appends cached ones via `items.update(cache_items)`, and missing ids may be absent. WHY: when some error events are cached and others are not, or when ids repeat, each ErrorEvent gets another event's id, and once misaligned the title/message/timestamp sent to Seer can belong to the wrong id. HOW: look up by node id instead: `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids): data = events.get(node_id); if data is None: continue; ...`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: error timestamps from nodestore (seconds as a float) are compared directly with the top-level rrweb event `timestamp`, which as_log_message also reads (event_parser.py:182) and which is in milliseconds for recorded replay events. WHY: every real error timestamp is about 1000x smaller than the breadcrumb timestamps, so all errors are emitted before all breadcrumbs and the chronological interleaving this change is meant to add does not happen. The tests pass only because they put seconds into the top-level field. HOW: convert to one unit before comparing, e.g. compare `error['timestamp'] * 1000` against the event timestamp, or normalize both to seconds.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: every request (including each paginated page) now runs a Snuba replay query and an unbounded `nodestore.get_multi` over all of the replay's error_ids before pagination happens. WHY: replays with many errors trigger a large nodestore fetch on every page request, which adds latency and load that scale with the replay's error count. HOW: cap the number of error_ids fetched (e.g. the first N by timestamp), and/or fetch only when the page actually needs them.

suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness (`if self.initial_data.get("age")` / `.get("timestamp")`), so a report with `age: 0` plus a timestamp, or `timestamp: 0` plus age, is accepted. A report with neither field also passes because both are optional. WHY: reports that mix the two spec formats, or carry neither time field, are accepted even though the validators are meant to reject them. HOW: use `"age" in self.initial_data` and `"timestamp" in self.initial_data`, and add a `validate()` that requires exactly one of the two.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Mutual-exclusion check between age and timestamp uses truthiness, so a value of 0 is treated as absent.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `validate_timestamp` uses `if self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` uses `if self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. A report with `age: 0` and a timestamp, or with `timestamp: 0` (allowed by min_value=0) and an age, passes validation even though the two fields are meant to be mutually exclusive. Check whether the key is present instead, for example `if "age" in self.initial_data` / `if self.initial_data.get("age") is not None`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the dict returned by get_multi matches error_ids one-to-one and in order.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. The code pairs `error_ids` with `events.values()` by position. If `error_ids` contains a duplicate, the dict has fewer entries and every id after it gets the wrong event's title, message and timestamp. Any backend that builds the dict in a different order (for example cache hits first) causes the same mix-up. Look up each event by its own node id instead: `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Error ids are paired with nodestore results by position instead of by the node_id key, so they can end up attached to the wrong events.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node_id. The code then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, which assumes the dict iterates in the same order as `error_ids` and contains every id. If the backend builds the dict from cache hits first and backend fetches second, or leaves out ids it didn't find, every later id shifts and each ErrorEvent gets another event's id. Look each one up by its own node_id instead: `[ErrorEvent(id=eid, ...) for eid, nid in zip(error_ids, node_ids) if (data := events.get(nid)) is not None]`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Zipping error_ids with get_multi().values() assumes the result is in request order, which may not hold, so error data can end up attached to the wrong id.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id. The code assumes that dict lists events in the same order as `error_ids`, which may not hold: if, as I expect, cached entries are added before backend fetches, the order changes. Duplicate error IDs also collapse into one key and shift every later pair. Either way an error's id can be paired with another event's title, message and timestamp. Look each event up by its own node_id instead of relying on position.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for processes created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, so a hung process is never killed. Those objects are `SpawnProcess`, which subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process`. WHY: on a 'hang' restart, the old flusher keeps running, and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second process for the same shards that shares the same healthy_since/backpressure Values. Two flushers then produce the same segments twice and race on `done_flush_segments`, and stuck processes pile up with each restart. The old code called `kill()` unconditionally. HOW: call `process.kill()` when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or use `hasattr(process, 'kill')`, keeping the ValueError guard.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: in join(), when the deadline expires the loop `break`s before reaching the remaining processes, so they are never terminated. The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` check is also False for SpawnProcess, so terminate() never runs for any process. WHY: on shutdown or rebalance with a timeout, flusher processes for other shards keep running and flushing after the consumer thinks they are stopped. HOW: always terminate every process. For example, loop over all processes, skip only the waiting step when the deadline has passed, and use `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`.

suggestions.label: performance
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: submit() now calls `get_memory_info()` and `record_stored_segments()` once per per-process buffer. `get_memory_info` is `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)` (buffer.py:376), which queries the whole Redis cluster no matter which shards the buffer owns. WHY: every submit on the main consumer thread now makes N cluster-wide INFO round-trips plus N ZCARD pipelines instead of one each, and memory figures are counted N times. That adds main-thread latency, which this PR is meant to reduce. HOW: keep one SpansBuffer for all assigned shards in the parent for record_stored_segments/get_memory_info, and use the per-process buffers only inside the child processes.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: each process gets `SpansBuffer(shards)` with only its subset of shards, and flush_segments computes `max_segments_per_shard = ceil(max-flush-segments / len(assigned_shards))` (buffer.py:382-384) per buffer. WHY: the `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` limit used to be global across all assigned shards. It now applies per process, so the total flushed per cycle is up to num_processes times the configured limit, which changes the memory/throughput bound operators rely on.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `wait_produce` tags the shard list as `shards`, while the sibling metrics use `shard` for the same value.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The same `shard_tag` value is sent under the tag key `"shard"` for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `segment_size_bytes` (lines 185 and 195), but under `"shards"` for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199). Dashboards and queries that filter on one key will silently miss the other metric. Use one consistent key name.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The new `time.sleep(0.1)` is a no-op because the test patches `time.sleep` at line 15, so nothing waits for the flusher thread to flush before `join()` stops it.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment says the sleep gives the flusher threads time to process after the drift change. But line 15 patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None`, so `time.sleep(0.1)` returns immediately and does no waiting. `step.join()` then sets `stopped=True` at once. If the flusher thread hasn't yet run a loop pass with `current_drift=9000`, it leaves `while not stopped.value` without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. Whether the test passes depends on thread scheduling. Wait on a condition instead of a patched sleep. For example, poll with a deadline until `messages` is non-empty, using the real sleep saved before patching, and only then call `step.join()`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: A hung flusher process is never killed before its replacement starts, so two processes flush the same shards at once.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The guard `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never True for the spawned flusher processes. They are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects, which subclass `BaseProcess` and not `multiprocessing.Process`. As a result, when a process is restarted because of a hang, it is never killed. It keeps calling `flush_segments` on its shards while the new process does the same, so segments can be flushed and produced twice. Both processes also write to the same shared `healthy_since`/`backpressure_since` Values, which can hide whether the replacement is actually healthy. The old code called `kill()` unconditionally. The fix is to check for the thread case instead.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for SpawnProcess, so a hung flusher process is never killed before it is restarted.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Processes come from `self.mp_context.Process`, where `mp_context` is the spawn context, so each one is a `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. That class is based on `BaseProcess` and is not a subclass of `multiprocessing.Process`, so this check is always False. Before this PR, `kill()` was called unconditionally. Now, in the 'hang' case, the old process keeps running while a new one starts for the same shards. Both then flush the same segments, and the restart doesn't do what it is meant to. Fix: check `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess)`, or skip only threads (`not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`). The same problem affects the `terminate()` check in `join()`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Sibling flusher metrics use different tag keys: `shard` on produce/segment_size_bytes and `shards` on wait_produce.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged `shard=shard_tag`, but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged `shards=shard_tag`. All three are emitted from the same loop with the same value. A dashboard or query that filters on one key will miss the other metric. Use one key for all of them.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: When the deadline expires, `join()` breaks out of the loop and never calls `terminate()` on the remaining processes.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Once `remaining_time <= 0`, the `break` exits the loop, so `terminate()` is never called for the remaining processes. In the old single-process code, `terminate()` always ran after the wait. Now, a timed-out shutdown can leave flusher processes running. Fix: skip only the wait when the deadline has passed, and still terminate every process.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The docstring says the flusher creates one process per shard, but the process count is capped by `max_processes` (CLI default 1) and shards share processes.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." That is not what the code does. `num_processes = min(self.max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` (line 60), and shards are assigned round-robin across that many processes (lines 64-66). The `--flusher-processes` option defaults to 1, so in the default setup a single process flushes every assigned shard. Suggested wording: "Creates up to `max_processes` processes and distributes the assigned shards among them round-robin."

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `_create_process_for_shard` is newly added but never called.
suggestions.suggestionContent: Nothing in this PR calls `_create_process_for_shard`; restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards` directly. Remove it, or use it in the restart path.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once, when the module is imported, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` (including all instances from `from_integration` and from `from_dict` with no `queued` key) shares the same stale worker-start timestamp. WHY: `queued` does not record when the assignment was queued, so any ordering, debouncing, or staleness logic built on it will be wrong, and test_to_dict only asserts `is not None`, which hides the problem. HOW: use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (import `field` from dataclasses).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: the cycle check compares only `integration_id`, so outbound sync is skipped for every external issue on the source integration, not only the issue that triggered the webhook. WHY: when a group is linked to two issues on the same Jira/VSTS integration (for example APP-1 and APP-2), an inbound assignee change from APP-1 no longer reaches APP-2, which silently drops a sync that worked before this PR. HOW: also carry the originating external issue key or id in AssignmentSource and skip only when it matches the target external_issue.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: `assignment_source` is added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature, but no caller passes it and the inbound status path (sync_status_inbound) never builds an AssignmentSource. WHY: status changes can still loop between Sentry and the integration, and the new parameter is never used, so this change suggests cycle protection for status syncs that does not exist.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The `queued` field doesn't hold the queue time: its default `timezone.now()` runs once at import.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The field name `queued` says it is the time this assignment source was created or queued. But `timezone.now()` as a dataclass default runs only once, at module import. Every AssignmentSource built by `from_integration` gets the process start time, which is wrong and misleading for anyone reading `queued` downstream. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` and import `field` from dataclasses.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: `queued` defaults to a single timestamp taken when the module is imported, not the time each assignment source is created.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs once, when the class is defined. Every AssignmentSource created afterwards without an explicit `queued` (including every `from_integration` call) gets the same timestamp: the time the process imported this module. The field is supposed to say when an assignment was queued, but it never does. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets the time it was created.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The default for `queued` is computed once at import time, so every AssignmentSource gets the same old timestamp.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The default `timezone.now()` runs once, when the class is defined at module import, not each time an instance is created. Every `AssignmentSource.from_integration(...)` and every `AssignmentSource(...)` built without an explicit `queued` therefore shares the process start time. That wrong timestamp is then written into every task payload by `to_dict()`, so `queued` is always incorrect and gets more out of date the longer the worker or web process runs. Use `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` and import `field` from dataclasses.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: test_to_dict asserts queued is not None, which is always true, so the import-time timezone.now() default goes undetected.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` (assignment_source.py:18) is evaluated once, when the class is defined. Every AssignmentSource therefore shares the timestamp from process start. The test only checks `result.get("queued") is not None`, which holds for any default, so it would still pass with this bug present or with any wrong value. Assert something about the value itself: that it falls between timestamps taken just before and after construction, or that two instances created at different times get different `queued` values. Then switch the field to `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so that the stronger test passes.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Test names do not match their bodies: 'empty_array' passes an empty dict, and 'inalid' is misspelled.
suggestions.suggestionContent: test_from_dict_empty_array passes `{}`, not an array, so a non-dict input such as a list is never tested. test_from_dict_inalid_data has a typo, so a run filtered on 'invalid' will not pick it up. Rename them to test_from_dict_empty_dict and test_from_dict_invalid_data, or change the first test to really pass a list if that case matters.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every existing Integration has sender metadata. build_integration (lines 376-377) only sets `metadata['sender']` when `state.get('sender')` is present, and installation.py:44 explicitly handles its absence. For an Integration created without sender (pipeline-created, or created before this metadata existed) that has no OrganizationIntegration left, this line raises KeyError and the setup view returns a 500 instead of a controlled response. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`, and render `error(...)` when it is missing or does not match.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.suggestionContent: The new GitHub-user verification (lines 501-505) only runs when an Integration row already exists. In the `Integration.DoesNotExist` branch, `pipeline.next_step()` is called without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to the installer. If the pipeline finishes before the `installation` webhook creates the Integration, any authenticated GitHub user who supplies an `installation_id` can bind that installation to their Sentry org, so the protection depends on webhook ordering. Verify the installer in this branch as well (for example, check the authenticated user against the installation's account/sender from the GitHub API) or fail closed.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `safe_urlopen(...)` is called outside the try/except, and `get_user_info` calls `resp.raise_for_status()` (identity/github/provider.py:16) with no handling. A network failure during the token exchange, or a non-2xx from `https://api.github.com/user` (revoked or invalid token, rate limit), therefore raises out of dispatch as a 500 instead of rendering the `github-integration-failed.html` error page. Wrap both calls in the try block and return `error(request, self.active_organization)` on exception.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Short error messages passed to error() as plain strings are no longer marked for translation, so they stop being extracted for translators.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `error()` translates `error_short` at runtime with `_(error_short)`, but every caller passes a plain string: the default "Invalid installation request." and the strings at lines 471 and 488. Before this change those messages were literals inside `_()`, so makemessages extracted them. Now they are not in the catalogs, so `_()` has nothing to look up and they always show in English. To fix this, mark the literals at the source, either with `gettext_noop`/`_()` on the default and at each call site, or by passing already-lazy strings and dropping the `_()` around `error_short`.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Direct indexing of integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises KeyError when the integration has no stored sender.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `integration.metadata` may not have a `sender` key. integration.py:376 only stores it conditionally, and installation.py:44 already handles the case where it is missing. Reading `metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly raises KeyError, so the request fails with a 500 instead of showing the error page. Use safe lookups and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Indexing integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] raises a KeyError for integrations that have no sender metadata.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `integration.metadata["sender"]` is not always present. build_integration (integration.py:376-377) stores it only when `state.get("sender")` is set, and installation.py:44 explicitly handles a missing `sender`. When an active Integration has no OrganizationIntegration and no sender metadata, this line raises an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500) instead of rendering the error page. Use a safe lookup so a missing sender is treated as a mismatch.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: New sender-login check indexes `metadata["sender"]` without a guard, but `sender` is optional in integration metadata, so the request crashes with a `KeyError`.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This branch handles an Integration that exists but has no OrganizationIntegration. It used to always move on to `pipeline.next_step()`. Now it reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. Other code treats `sender` as optional: it is set conditionally at line 376-377, and `installation.py:44` checks for it. When an integration has no `sender` in its metadata, this raises `KeyError` and returns a 500 instead of the controlled error page. Use `.get()` and treat a missing sender as a verification failure.

suggestions.label: security
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The OAuth state is checked against the pipeline signature with a plain `!=` instead of a constant-time compare.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The OAuth `state` parameter is compared to `pipeline.signature` with a plain `!=`. A normal string compare stops at the first differing character, so its timing can leak how much of the session-bound value an attacker has guessed. The rest of the codebase uses `django.utils.crypto.constant_time_compare` for tokens and signatures (for example github/webhook.py:587 and auth/superuser.py:271). Use it here too, and treat a missing state as a failure.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Indexing `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly raises a KeyError (a 500) for integrations whose metadata has no sender.
suggestions.suggestionContent: If an existing Integration has no `sender` in its metadata (it is only set when `state.get("sender")` is present, and installation.py:44 already handles it being missing), this comparison raises a KeyError and the request returns a 500. The user should get the 'Invalid installation request' dialog instead. Use `.get()` lookups and send a missing sender to the error page.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: test_installation_not_found fails at the OAuth state check before it ever reaches the 404 installation lookup, so it no longer tests installation-not-found handling.
suggestions.suggestionContent: test_installation_not_found no longer tests what its name says. The OAuth callback sends state 'ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05', which doesn't match the pipeline signature, so OAuthLoginView returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error at the state check (integration.py:412). The flow never reaches GitHubInstallation or the `/app/installations/{id}` call that the 404 stub is meant to hit. The assertion was also loosened from 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' to the generic error. As written, the test would still pass if installation-not-found handling were broken or deleted. Fix: start the pipeline via init_path with installation_id, finish the OAuth step with the valid signature state, and assert the specific not-found message again.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but has only a `pass` body. It does not implement the abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` or the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, so it is still an abstract class. WHY: `Detector.detector_handler` instantiates `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, so any `metric_alert_fire` detector raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. `process_detectors` does not catch this, so the whole batch of detectors fails. Before this PR the old handler safely returned []. HOW: implement the abstract methods (they can be stubs that return safe defaults, e.g. `counter_names = []`, `get_group_key_values` returning {}), or keep the previous non-stateful stub until the real implementation lands.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: WHAT: build_mock_occurrence_and_event always uses the same hardcoded `id`, and `IssueOccurrence.__eq__` compares only `id` (issue_occurrence.py:181-184). WHY: none of the new occurrence assertions check the fingerprint, group key or priority. For example, TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence for 'val1' but evaluates 'group_key', and still passes. In test_state_results_multi_group, `occurrence` and `occurrence_2` compare as equal, so the `produce_occurrence_to_kafka` assertions can't detect the wrong occurrence being sent for a group. HOW: generate a distinct id per call (e.g. derived from group_key), and/or assert on `fingerprint` and `initial_issue_priority` explicitly.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with only `pass`, so it does not implement the abstract methods: build_occurrence_and_event_data (added in this PR), get_dedupe_value and get_group_key_values. Instantiating the handler, which happens when Detector.detector_handler is accessed for a metric-alert detector in process_detectors, will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. Before this change, evaluate() had a concrete stub that returned []. Fix: implement the abstract methods (stubs are fine for now), or keep a concrete evaluate() that returns {} until the handler is built out.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods (including the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data), so instantiating it raises TypeError.
suggestions.suggestionContent: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was moved from DetectorHandler, where it implemented evaluate as a stub, to StatefulDetectorHandler with only `pass`. StatefulDetectorHandler has abstract methods get_dedupe_value and get_group_key_values, and this PR adds a third, build_occurrence_and_event_data. The subclass implements none of them, so `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises TypeError. Any metric-alert detector reaching Detector.detector_handler / process_detectors would crash instead of being a harmless no-op. Implement the abstract methods, even as stubs, or keep the previous DetectorHandler-based stub until the stateful version is ready.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The mock occurrence builder ignores `value`, so no test checks that the evaluated value reaches `build_occurrence_and_event_data`.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` takes `value` but never puts it into the occurrence or the event data. Several tests build their expected occurrence with `value=6` even though the code under test sees 10, 100 or 8: `test_state_results_multi_group`'s group_2, `TestEvaluate.test_results_on_change`, `TestEvaluate.test_dedupe` and `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe`. They pass only because the value is dropped. If `evaluate_group_key_value` stopped forwarding the evaluated value correctly to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, for example by passing `dedupe_value` or a constant instead, every test would still pass. Fix: include `value` in the mock occurrence, e.g. `evidence_data={"value": value}`, and pass the actual value each test uses when building the expected result.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing its abstract methods, including the new build_occurrence_and_event_data, so creating it raises TypeError.
suggestions.suggestionContent: In processors/detector.py, `StatefulDetectorHandler` gains a new abstract method, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. It also requires `get_dedupe_value` and `get_group_key_values`. `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses it with only `pass`, and the concrete `evaluate` it used to have was removed. The class is therefore still abstract. When `Detector.detector_handler` creates the handler for a metric-alert detector, Python raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. That breaks process_detectors for these detectors. Add stub implementations, or keep the class off the abstract base until it is implemented.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: evaluate() docstring still says it returns a list, but it now returns a dict keyed by group key.
suggestions.suggestionContent: This PR changed `evaluate` to return `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but the docstring still says it "returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`". Someone reading it may index or iterate the result as a list. Update the docstring to describe the dict keyed by group key. Because results are now keyed by group key, the old duplicate-key handling is gone.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: Stale TODO says the handler will become stateful, but it now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler.
suggestions.suggestionContent: The comment "TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" is no longer true. This PR makes MetricAlertDetectorHandler a subclass of StatefulDetectorHandler. Remove the TODO, or reword it to say what is actually still missing (e.g. implementing get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values and build_occurrence_and_event_data).

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.suggestionContent: `PriorityLevel(new_status)` converts a DetectorPriorityLevel to PriorityLevel by value. If any non-OK DetectorPriorityLevel value has no matching PriorityLevel member, this raises ValueError during evaluation and aborts processing for every group key in the packet. Use an explicit mapping, or check that the enum values match.

suggestions.label: bug
suggestions.oneSentenceSummary: The transformed `config` copy (with the human-readable schedule_type) is computed but never used; the returned context contains the raw `monitor.config` instead.
suggestions.suggestionContent: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor.config` into `config` and replaces `schedule_type` with `get_schedule_type_display()`. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`, so the copy and the substitution are thrown away. As a result, the monitor context attached to every incident occurrence shows the raw integer schedule_type, not the readable label. Fix: return `config` in the `"config"` key.
